title: Manhwa Meta — Ink & Hangul Thunder
description: A webtoon-panel slide modeled on Naver and Kakao episode intros — tall vertical framing, deep-ink character silhouette, and oversized Hangul onomatopoeia that hits like a first-chapter splash page.
philosophy: This template exists to transplant manhwa panel grammar directly into slide decks, not merely dress corporate layouts in Korean typefaces. It rejects horizontal symmetry and safe whitespace, demanding the diagonal tension and tall-crop rhythm native to mobile-scroll webtoon reading. The speaker is cast as the episode auteur, not the presenter — every compositional choice privileges kinetic impact over information density. It assumes the audience has swiped through at least one webtoon chapter and will recognize the visual contract immediately.
goodFor: Opening hero slides for entertainment IP or webtoon brand pitches
Episode-framed narrative presentations built around a single dramatic reveal
Youth-targeted campaign or product launch announcements
Creative portfolio intro slides where first impression is the entire argument
avoidFor: Chart-heavy quarterly business reviews requiring multi-column data layout
Academic or research paper presentations demanding neutral hierarchy
B2B enterprise sales decks where formal tone is non-negotiable
Text-dense informational slides with more than three lines of body copy
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel like the opening splash panel of a Naver webtoon chapter — kinetic, ink-saturated, and slightly overwhelming in the best way. Composition follows a diagonal thrust from lower-right to upper-left, with a deep silhouette figure half-swallowed by the frame edge generating raw asymmetric tension. Massive Hangul onomatopoeia letterforms erupt behind the title like a thunder-strike overlay, carrying visible ink bleed and brushstroke roughness. Reject centered layouts, horizontal symmetry, and any breathing whitespace — this slide should feel as though it is already mid-action when the audience first sees it.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid with a deliberate bleed break — the ink silhouette enters from the right edge and dominates cols 6–12, hard-cropped against the frame with no containment margin. Title copy stacks in cols 1–5 at upper-third placement, hierarchy driven by size contrast alone with no rule lines or banding. Oversized Hangul SFX letterforms sweep diagonally across cols 3–11 as a mid-depth layer sitting between the background field and the title text. No header band; episode or deck identifier sits flush to the bottom-left corner at minimum scale.

examples.promptCore: The slide feels like a mid-chapter webtoon reveal panel — kinetic and confrontational, as if the information itself just slammed onto the screen mid-swipe. Ink-splatter texture and diagonal panel tension hold the composition together, with the content payload framed like a character stat card or episode-chapter annotation overlay. The mood is urgent and authorial, not explanatory. Avoid centered symmetry, soft gradients, and anything resembling a corporate infographic — every element should feel torn directly from a Naver episode drop, not assembled in a slide editor.
